item.title: WhisperX Updates With Context-Aware Batching and CUDA Toolkit 12.8 Support
item.description:
WhisperX Updates With Context-Aware Batching and CUDA Toolkit 12.8 Support

WhisperX has received new developments including the release of Context-Aware Batching in 2026 and CUDA toolkit 12.8 installation guidelines.

🚀 Availability

  • The easiest way to install WhisperX is through PyPi: pip install whisperx
  • Alternatively, use uvx: uvx whisperx
  • For Linux users, install the CUDA toolkit 12.8 following the provided guide
  • For Windows users, download and install the CUDA toolkit 12.8
  • To use WhisperX with GPU acceleration, install the CUDA toolkit 12.8 before WhisperX
  • Additional dependencies may include ffmpeg, rust, etc.

⚙️ Key details

  • Context-Aware Batching Released 2026: Enables condition_on_previous_context within the batched transcription framework, improving punctuation and proper noun adherence
  • Uses faster-whisper backend, requiring <8GB gpu memory for large-v2 with beam_size=5
  • Accurate word-level timestamps using wav2vec2 alignment
  • Multispeaker ASR using speaker diarization from pyannote-audio (speaker ID labels)
  • VAD preprocessing, reduces hallucination & batching with no WER degradation

#WhisperX #SpeechRecognition #AI #MachineLearning

Source: m-bain/whisperX

item.title: Reson8 Open Sources Rumble-2-Flash: A 0.5B Speech Recognition Model
item.description:
Reson8 Open Sources Rumble-2-Flash: A 0.5B Speech Recognition Model

Reson8 has open-sourced Rumble-2-Flash, a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model, under the Apache 2.0 license. Designed for 40+ languages, the model competes with systems 3-60x its size while offering native support in Hugging Face Transformers and vLLM without requiring custom code.

🧩 How it works

Rumble-2-Flash utilizes the Qwen3-ASR architecture to ensure day-0 support. To determine how small a model could become before accuracy degraded, the team distilled Rumble-2, a larger production model, into this smaller version using on-policy distillation.

In this process, the student model does not train on transcripts written by the teacher. Instead, it transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token. At every position, the teacher provides its own probability for the next token, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it receives corrections for the specific mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token rather than a single score per clip.

On-policy distillation typically requires the teacher and student to share a tokenizer, which was not the case here. Choosing Qwen3-ASR meant adopting its vocabulary, so the team introduced GOLD to remove this restriction. GOLD merges tokens where the two tokenizers split text differently, allowing both models to be compared over the same text. Tokens present in both vocabularies are compared directly, while others are compared via their sorted probabilities.

⚙️ Key details

  • Languages: Supports 40+ languages with automatic language detection.
  • Output Control: Allows numbers as digits or words, management of fillers, verbatim repeats, and forced language settings.
  • Performance: Processes an hour of audio in about half a second, achieving over 7,000 RTFx on full batches.
  • Benchmarking: On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track (Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch, and English), it averages a 6.96% error rate.
  • Comparison: This performance is better than Meta’s omniASR-LLM 7B (15x larger) and ahead of Whisper large-v3.
  • English Track: Averages a 6.6% WER.

On AppTek’s call-centre benchmark, which includes 302 hours of helpline calls and 14 English accents, Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER. This result is on par with NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78% and well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%). It is close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that performs better.

Model Performance Context
Rumble-2-Flash 7.86% WER on AppTek call-centre benchmark
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe 7.78% WER (On par with Rumble-2-Flash)
Qwen3-ASR 0.6B 8.7% WER
Qwen3-ASR 1.7B 7.4% WER

🚀 Availability

The model weights are available on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code required.

#Reson8 #SpeechRecognition #OpenSource #LLM #Qwen3

Source: Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

item.title: Speaches provides an OpenAI-compatible API for speech-to-text and text-to-speech
item.description:
Speaches provides an OpenAI-compatible API for speech-to-text and text-to-speech

Speaches is an OpenAI API-compatible server that supports streaming transcription, translation, and speech generation.

🔍 Overview

  • The project aims to be the equivalent of Ollama, but specifically for TTS/STT models.
  • It is OpenAI API compatible, meaning all tools and SDKs that work with OpenAI’s API should work with speaches.
  • Supports GPU and CPU environments.
  • Deployable via Docker Compose or Docker.
  • Highly configurable.
  • Includes a Realtime API.

🧩 How it works

  • Speech-to-Text: Powered by faster-whisper.
  • Text-to-Speech: Uses piper and Kokoro models.
  • Streaming: Transcription is sent via SSE as the audio is transcribed; users do not need to wait for the audio to fully be transcribed before receiving it.
  • Dynamic Model Loading: Users specify which model to use in the request, and it is loaded automatically. The model is unloaded after a period of inactivity.

💡 Why it matters

Speaches enables specific audio-to-text and text-to-audio workflows:

  • Generate a spoken audio summary of a body of text (text in, audio out).
  • Perform sentiment analysis on a recording (audio in, text out).
  • Support async speech-to-speech interactions with a model (audio in, audio out).

#OpenAI #SpeechRecognition #TextToSpeech #Docker #API

Source: speaches-ai/speaches

item.title: Open ASR Leaderboard Adds Egyptian and Nigerian Private Data Splits
item.description:
Open ASR Leaderboard Adds Egyptian and Nigerian Private Data Splits

A new collaboration with Liva AI expands the Open ASR Leaderboard with two private, conversational English splits for Egyptian 🇪🇬 and Nigerian 🇳🇬 accents, continuing the effort to improve representation and trust in automatic‑speech‑recognition evaluation.

🔎 Overview

  • Earlier this year the leaderboard added private data: 11 splits from Appen and DataOceanAI covering scripted and conversational speech from five accents.
  • The community praised the held‑out sets for enabling trustworthy evaluations.
  • A subsequent addition introduced a private split for Indian‑accented English supplied by Voice Arena.
  • The latest update introduces two new accents via Liva AI.

📊 New Private Splits

Dataset Accent Duration (hrs) Speech Type Transcription
Liva AI Conversational EG Egyptian 1.34 Conversational, spontaneous Punctuated, cased, with disfluencies
Liva AI Conversational NG Nigerian 1.55 Conversational, spontaneous Punctuated, cased, with disfluencies

🌍 Representation & Trust

  • The leaderboard now reports a richer breakdown of accents using Kachru’s Three Circles framework (credit to Hume AI for the idea).
  • As more accents join, the Outer and Expanding Circles will be split to reflect finer granularity.
  • Adding new private splits helps minimise “bench‑maxxing” and provides more reliable, held‑out evaluation data.

🛠️ How Liva AI Contributes

  • Liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people.
  • Owning both the collection environment and distribution lets Liva design products that target specific model gaps across domains, industries, languages, modalities, and interaction types.
  • This approach yields natural, high‑context behavior that emerges from real product use, rather than from artificially elicited or task‑based interactions.

📈 Why it matters

  • More accents and languages improve the global relevance of ASR benchmarks.
  • Private, high‑quality data supports the community in pushing ASR performance for the world 🤗

#ASR #OpenLeaderboard #DataDiversity #SpeechRecognition

Source: Egyptian and Nigerian English join the Open ASR Leaderboard

item.title: AnyLanguageModel adds on‑device speech and decision packages for Swift
item.description:
AnyLanguageModel adds on‑device speech and decision packages for Swift

Today the AnyLanguageModel project announced two new Swift packages — AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel — that extend its 1.x Swift API approach to speech transcription and decision‑making while keeping a familiar Apple‑style API.

🔍 Overview

  • AnySpeechRecognizer implements Apple’s new SpeechAnalyzer API but lets you pick the underlying engine, including NVIDIA’s Parakeet and Alibaba’s Qwen3‑ASR running locally via Core ML.
  • It adds speaker diarization to track who is speaking when.
  • AnyDecisionModel answers yes‑or‑no, multiple‑choice, and rating‑scale questions, returning typed results and probabilities derived from model logits rather than generated text.
  • Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them entirely on‑device.

🗣️ AnySpeechRecognizer

  • Mirrors Apple’s SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory components.
  • Uses Apple’s Speech framework as the default engine; swapping to a different engine only requires changing the import.
  • Supports file‑based and live audio input, volatile results, word timing, and confidence scores when the selected engine provides them.
  • Includes built‑in speaker diarization.

🤖 AnyDecisionModel

  • Provides typed answers (yes/no, multiple‑choice, rating‑scale) with associated probabilities.
  • Derives answers from model probabilities, not from text generation.
  • Runs on‑device with MLX, Core AI, llama.cpp, or a decision model from Jev or Ollama.
  • Can be integrated with the same Swift API style used for language and speech models.

📦 Model Options

Model Size(s) Languages / Dialects Notable Traits
Parakeet v3 (NVIDIA) 0.6 B 25 European languages (auto‑detect locale) Runs on Core ML runtime, supports file & live input, volatile results, word timing, confidence
Parakeet Ultra (Moondream) 0.6 B (post‑trained) Same as v3 More accurate in most measurements
Parakeet Unified (NVIDIA) – English only –
Qwen3‑ASR (Alibaba) 0.6 B, 1.7 B 30 languages + 22 Chinese dialects (Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, Korean) Provides a single final result per ≤40 s segment, no volatile results, no word timing or confidence, runs on GPU, slower than Parakeet, better for file transcription

⚙️ How it works

  • You create a SpeechAnalyzer (or AnySpeechRecognizer) and attach modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector.
  • Provide an audio file or a stream of audio buffers; results are delivered via asynchronous sequences as they become available.
  • AssetInventory handles model installation; downloads occur only when the app requests them.
  • Models are stored in the standard Hugging Face cache, allowing a macOS app outside the sandbox to share them with Python or other Hugging Face tools.

🚀 Availability

  • Packages are available as Swift packages; they depend on the 1.x releases of AnyLanguageModel and swift‑huggingface.
  • Approximate download sizes (per model):
    • Parakeet variants: ~600 MB each + ~590 MB for the live encoder.
    • Qwen3‑ASR: 0.9 GB to 2.4 GB depending on model size.
    • Sortformer (used for speaker diarization): ~250 MB.
  • Once downloaded, models run entirely on‑device, with no ongoing cloud usage required.

#Swift #SpeechRecognition #OnDeviceAI #MachineLearning

Source: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

item.title: Word Duration Directly Cues Word Identity in Mandarin Homophones
item.description:
Word Duration Directly Cues Word Identity in Mandarin Homophones

A new study shows that listeners can use the length of a spoken word to identify it, even when other cues are unavailable.

🔍 Overview

  • The research investigates whether word‑level phonetic cues, specifically word duration, are stored in the mental lexicon and can influence spoken word recognition.
  • Across languages, including Mandarin Chinese, high‑frequency words tend to be shorter than low‑frequency words.

🧩 How it works

  • Researchers used a homophone ordering task with Mandarin Chinese, a language rich in disyllabic homophones.
  • Participants heard pairs of homophones that differed in lexical frequency and were asked to identify the order.
  • The only systematic difference between the stimuli was word duration.

⚙️ Key details

  • Participants reliably mapped the shorter‑duration auditory stimulus to the higher‑frequency word.
  • This mapping held even under high noise levels and when no other cues were available.
  • Results indicate that word duration can serve as a direct cue to word identity, suggesting it may be a phonetic detail incorporated into lexical representations.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides evidence that the mental lexicon stores specific phonetic details (duration) that are functionally relevant for word recognition.
  • Supports a “direct cueing” account of how duration influences lexical access, alongside alternative explanations.

#Psycholinguistics #Mandarin #WordDuration #SpeechRecognition

Source: Direct cueing of word identity through word duration: evidence from Mandarin homophones

item.title: IBM Updates Granite Speech Collection with New Multilingual and High-Speed Models
item.description:
IBM Updates Granite Speech Collection with New Multilingual and High-Speed Models

IBM has announced three updates to its Granite Speech collection: a new speech-language model called granite-speech-5.0-2b, and revised versions of granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc and granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus. These models are designed to cover enterprise speech requirements, including high-accuracy transcription, translation, and long-form multi-speaker analysis.

🔍 Overview

Model Primary Use Case Key Attributes
granite-speech-5.0-2b High-accuracy work 2B parameters, multilingual transcription and translation, keyword biasing
granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc Raw speed or edge use 470M parameters, 19,870 RTFx speed, native punctuation
granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus Meetings and multi-speaker calls Speaker attribution, tighter timestamps, 24% lower long-form WER

⚙️ Key details

granite-speech-5.0-2b

This model is the successor to granite-speech-4.1-2b and maintains the same parameter count. It was trained on 390,000 hours of public audio alongside synthetic data for Japanese ASR, translation, and keyword biasing.

  • Multilingual Capabilities: Transcribes English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese. Translates to and from English for those languages, plus English to Italian and Mandarin.
  • Advanced Prompting: Supports Language ID prompting and allows users to request formatted output; capitalization F1 ranges from 89.7 to 99.5 across test sets.
  • Accuracy: Features improved handling of noise, reverberation, and distant-microphone speech.
  • Keyword Biasing: Supports lists of up to 2,000 terms to bias transcription toward product names and acronyms.

granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc

Formerly an English-only model, this 470M-parameter encoder is now optimized for speed and multilingual use.

  • Multilingual Expansion: Now supports English, Japanese, Spanish, German, French, Italian, and Portuguese.
  • Performance Gains: The model is approximately 1.6x faster than its launch version, reaching 19,870 RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard by reusing a compiled Conformer block graph.
  • Edge Readiness: Includes native punctuation and capitalization, and supports browser-based streaming via WebGPU.

granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus

This is a drop-in replacement for the original 4.1-2b model, utilizing the same architecture, API, and prompt format with improved weights for long-form enterprise recordings.

  • Speaker Attribution: The word diarization error rate (WDER) and speaker-attributed WER (cpWER) both decreased by 7%.
  • Timing Precision: The average timestamp shift (AAS) has been cut by more than half, improving captions and search.
  • Long-Speech Performance: WER on long-form test sets decreased by 24%, while keyword biasing errors fell 45% when using 20-term lists.

🚀 Availability

The models are released under the Apache 2.0 license and include support for:

  • Transformers and vLLM
  • llama.cpp
  • mlx-audio for Apple Silicon

#IBM #Granite #SpeechRecognition #MachineLearning #OpenSource

Source: Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster

item.title: Granite Switch 4.1 Unifies Chat, Decision‑Making and Speech on a Single Endpoint
item.description:
Granite Switch 4.1 Unifies Chat, Decision‑Making and Speech on a Single Endpoint

Granite Switch 4.1 introduces a family of models that pack chat, decision‑making and speech transcription capabilities into a single endpoint while using roughly the same GPU memory as the base model alone.

🔍 Overview

  • New model variants: Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑8B and Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑30B.
  • Each variant bundles three activated LoRA (aLoRA) adapters:
    • a Decision aLoRA for general‑purpose decision tasks (e.g., v1/systemone).
    • a Guardian aLoRA that, on average, outperforms Jev 1.13, Microsoft‑Decision‑1, GPT‑Luna‑Decisions and Clef‑Flash on safety‑related decision tasks.
    • Granite‑Speech‑5.0‑Turbo‑CTC, the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR Leaderboard, used for transcription.
  • The combined model occupies approximately the same VRAM as the underlying base model, delivering “more capabilities with fewer GPUs.”

🧩 How it works

  • The adapters are built as cache‑efficient Activated LoRAs. The KV cache generated by the base model during one generation can be reused for any subsequent adapter‑based request.
  • Recent vLLM contributions accelerate low‑rank adapter inference.
  • A co‑located ASR encoder enables the model to switch between chat, decision and spoken requests with “blazing fast speeds.”
  • An example Space – Speech‑to‑Decisions – shows granite-switch-4.1-8b transcribing audio, generating summaries, screening for harmful content and evaluating 15 user‑defined flags in real time on a single endpoint.

⚙️ Key details

Model Size Built‑in adapters
Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑8B 8 B parameters Decision aLoRA, Guardian aLoRA, Granite‑Speech‑5.0‑Turbo‑CTC
Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑30B 30 B parameters Decision aLoRA, Guardian aLoRA, Granite‑Speech‑5.0‑Turbo‑CTC
  • Performance: In a “race” against Jev‑27B (frozen Qwen base + 1 generic decision LoRA), Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑30B completed a real‑world, 5‑step RAG workflow faster.
  • Custom use case: A 3 B‑parameter Granite Switch model navigated the classic Doom game at 60–100 decisions / second, compared with Jev’s reported 10 decisions / second, and could also narrate and answer questions while playing.
  • Granite Libraries provide a repository of specialized adapters that can be mixed with the general‑purpose decision adapter at little extra cost because they share the base model’s KV cache.

🚀 Availability

  • The 8B and 30B models are released with “batteries included”, i.e., pre‑compiled with a helpful set of adapters.
  • Users may compose their own Granite Switch models by mixing adapters from Granite Libraries.
  • An Adapter SDK for training adapters in Mellea, along with tutorials and support, is planned for future release.

💡 Why it matters

  • Consolidates three major AI functionalities—chat, decision‑making and speech—into one model, simplifying deployment and reducing hardware requirements.
  • Cache‑efficient design and vLLM acceleration make multi‑modal switching real‑time, opening possibilities for interactive applications such as live transcription with instant safety screening.
  • The open‑adapter ecosystem encourages community extensions and custom task specialization without large memory overhead.

#GraniteSwitch #AIAdapters #SpeechRecognition #DecisionModels

Source: Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint

item.title: Study Improves Child Speech Recognition While Preserving Adult ASR Performance
item.description:
Study Improves Child Speech Recognition While Preserving Adult ASR Performance

Researchers have released an empirical study on adapting automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems for child speech while retaining adult performance.

🔍 Overview

  • Standard ASR models work well for adult speech but often underperform for children and non‑native speakers.
  • Directly adapting adult models to child speech can cause “adult‑speech forgetting,” degrading performance on existing adult benchmarks.

🧩 How it works

  • The study investigates child ASR adaptation with adult retention across Arabic and English.
  • Model families examined:
    • Encoder–decoder (e.g., Whisper)
    • Encoder–CTC
    • AudioLLM‑based ASR
  • Adaptation strategies compared:
    • Full fine‑tuning
    • LoRA (low‑rank adaptation)
    • Post‑hoc weight‑space merging (LERP and TIES)
  • Datasets:
    • Arabic native child speech
    • Arabic non‑native child speech
    • English MyST child speech
    • Adult benchmarks: MGB‑2 (Arabic) and LibriSpeech test‑clean (English)
  • Evaluation metrics: Word Error Rate (WER), Retention Index, Child Adaptation Gain, Adaptation Recovery.

⚙️ Key findings

  • Child adaptation is necessary, especially for non‑native Arabic and English child speech.
  • Direct adaptation often reduces adult ASR performance on the adult benchmarks.
  • Bilingual adaptation (training on both Arabic and English child data) yields a more stable trade‑off than language‑specific adaptation.
  • Weight‑space merging improves the adaptation‑retention balance:
    • Most effective for encoder–CTC, Whisper, and AudioLLM models.
    • LERP favours adult retention.
    • TIES recovers stronger child performance gains.
  • For the encoder–decoder model, direct bilingual fine‑tuning remains the strongest approach in raw WER.

📊 Trade‑off details

Adaptation method Effect on adult retention Effect on child gain
Full fine‑tuning May cause adult forgetting Improves child WER
LoRA Less adult impact than full fine‑tuning Improves child WER
Weight‑space merging (LERP) Keeps adult performance higher Moderate child gain
Weight‑space merging (TIES) Slight adult loss Stronger child gain

🚀 Availability

  • Code and pretrained models are released at the provided HTTPS URL (see the original paper).
  • The paper is titled “Child ASR Adaptation with Adult Retention: An Empirical Study” and was submitted on 25 Sep 2026 (v1).

#ASR #ChildSpeech #ModelAdaptation #SpeechRecognition

Source: Child ASR Adaptation with Adult Retention: An Empirical Study Source: When Forgetting Looks Like Improvement: Metric Masking in Streaming Diarizer Adaptation and the Price of Rehearsal Source: Dialect-Robust Speech Language Models with Synthetic Pseudo-Dialect Augmentation
